Work With Me

# Custom development, scoped and delivered

A WordPress plugin, an API integration, a payment fix, an AI feature. Described on Monday, delivered in about a week.

I'm a full-stack developer who ships production software — payment systems for enterprise clients, block-first WordPress, React and Node applications — and who runs two SaaS products of my own. You get one person who writes the code, owns the deploy, and is still around when something breaks.

Services

## What I do

Most projects touch more than one of these. That's the point — you don't have to coordinate between a dev shop, a WordPress contractor, an AI consultant, and an SEO agency.

[

### Custom AI integration

LLM features that survive real traffic — support agents, grounded answers over your content, and cost-controlled model routing. Claude, OpenAI, or self-hosted. Running in production on my own SaaS today.

### WordPress plugins & Gutenberg

Plugins and block-first builds written like software, not page-builder bloat. I've shipped 30+ custom React Gutenberg blocks for enterprise clients, a WPML multilingual RTL architecture, and two plugins live on WordPress.org, one of them a WooCommerce payment gateway.

### Web applications

Frontend and backend by the same person. React, Next.js, Node, TypeScript, PHP. Real-time features, Chrome extensions, and database migrations done without downtime.

### Integrations & automation

Making systems agree with each other, forever, without a human checking: third-party APIs, OAuth, webhooks with retries, CRM syncs, PDF generation, and the reconciliation nobody enjoys.

### SEO & organic growth

Technical SEO shipped by the person who diagnosed it — rendering and indexability, keyword architecture, internal link engineering, and page templates you can actually scale.

Why It Matters

## Shipping and being found are the same project

The usual split causes real damage. The dev team builds a fast single-page app with one URL, and there's nothing for Google to index. The SEO agency asks for thirty landing pages, and the dev team quotes six weeks because the templating wasn't built for it. Both are right. Neither owns the outcome.

When one person does both, the architecture decisions get made with search in mind from day one — URL structure, rendering strategy, internal linking, page templates you can actually extend. And when a keyword opportunity shows up eight months later, shipping the page takes an afternoon instead of a sprint.

I've done this on my own products, which is the honest reason I can claim it. [GhostChat](https://ghostchat.dev/), [Gmailytics](https://gmailytics.com/), and [KaspaWoo](https://kaspawoo.com/) were built, launched, and grown by one person — product and organic growth both.

Proof

## Shipped work, not a capabilities deck

Everything below is live, and most of it you can inspect yourself.

### 30+ custom Gutenberg blocks — and a generator to make more

At One Digital I built more than thirty React-based Gutenberg blocks for enterprise clients including Dimri, Sonol and Rishumit. Building them one at a time was the bottleneck, so I wrote a metadata-driven ACF block generator that produces the registration, fields and template from a single definition — it cut block development time by roughly 80%. That's the pattern I bring to WordPress work generally: if a task is going to happen fifty times, the second one should be generated, not typed. The same project ran WPML multilingual with Hebrew RTL and English LTR sharing components, which sounds like a CSS flag and turns out to touch layout, forms and every third-party embed.

### GhostChat — a SaaS with paying customers

[GhostChat](https://ghostchat.dev/) is a privacy-first chat widget with a ~15KB embeddable SDK: a Next.js dashboard on Vercel, a Cloudflare Workers API with Durable Objects for per-conversation state, Supabase for persistence and Stripe for billing. It ships with an AI responder running on Claude in production, a plugin on WordPress.org, and an open-source agent runner on npm. Scoped, built, launched and sold by one person. The chat widget on this page is that product.

### Gmailytics — OAuth at scale, independently security-audited

[Gmailytics](https://gmailytics.com/) is a web app plus Chrome extension that scans a Gmail inbox and bulk unsubscribes from unwanted senders. It has cleaned 5M+ emails and freed over 300GB of storage, and it's **Google CASA Tier 2 certified** — it passed an independent third-party security assessment for its use of restricted Gmail scopes, a bar most side projects never clear.

### Migrations that didn't take the site down

At Hertz Furniture I migrated a CRM of over 100,000 records to Salesforce with zero data loss and zero downtime, then built LiveChat bots and Salesforce webhooks that cut response time from hours to under ten minutes, and integrated Microsoft OneDrive via the Graph API for a 40% storage cost reduction. At Elphi I moved a production application from Firebase to PostgreSQL and added GraphQL subscriptions so the UI updated in real time.

**The thread running through all of it:** the interesting problems are rarely "build a form." They're "make these four systems agree with each other, forever, without a human checking." That's the work I like most and do best.

Selected Client Work

Alongside my own products, this is work I shipped as a developer at a digital agency and at a US company — for their clients, stated as outcomes rather than tech specs.

**30+ custom React-based Gutenberg blocks** plus an automated ACF block generator that **cut build time by 80%**, and a WPML multilingual architecture with full RTL/LTR support — delivered for named enterprise clients.

### Salesforce migration and workflow automation

Migrated **100K+ records** into Salesforce with the REST APIs and automated workflows around it. Integrated Microsoft Graph for OneDrive, **cutting storage costs 40%**, and implemented SignNow e-signatures that **reduced contract turnaround by 90%**. Delivered fully remote for a US company over two years.

### Looking after WordPress sites, not just building them

Managed and built three sites for an online media organisation: keeping WordPress, Elementor and plugins current, managing DNS, SSL and caching across cPanel and Cloudflare, and running the analytics and Search Console side — sitemaps, conversion tracking, and fixing what the data said was broken. That day-to-day upkeep is what the care plan below is.

How We Work Together

## Engagement models

Small, well-defined jobs have a fixed price. Larger builds are quoted after a conversation.

### Fixed-price build

One clearly scoped piece of work, done in about a week: a WordPress plugin or block-first Gutenberg build, an AI assistant or LLM feature wired to your content, a third-party API or webhook integration, a Stripe or WooCommerce payment fix, a performance rescue, a migration. You describe it, I confirm the scope in writing, half is paid to start and half on delivery. Smaller scoped jobs start at $500; a custom payment gateway starts at $1,200. Larger work is quoted.

**Typical** About 1 week · fixed price · 50% upfront

Describe the job

### Project build

A defined thing, delivered. A plugin, an integration, a marketing site, an MVP. Fixed scope, milestone-based, with a written spec before anyone writes code.

**Typical** 2–8 weeks · quoted

Tell me about the project

### Care plan

Keeping a WordPress site that already works from quietly falling over: updates with a backup first, monitoring, and up to three hours a month of fixes. What's included, what's extra, and how it works are on the [WordPress care page](https://jacoborbach.com/care/).

**Typical** $250/mo · up to 3 hours a month · catch-up quoted first if the site is badly out of date

[See the care plan](https://jacoborbach.com/care/)

### Ongoing retainer

A developer on your product every week, not just keeping the lights on — shipping new features, building out pages, and iterating on what the analytics and Search Console data say. This is where compounding growth happens.

**Typical** Monthly · capped hours · from $2,000/mo

Talk about a retainer

### Audit & rescue

Something is broken, slow, or silently losing you traffic. I diagnose it, document what I find, and either hand you the fix list or implement it.

**Typical** 3–10 days · fixed price

Book an audit

Process

## What working with me looks like

- **A real conversation first** Thirty minutes on what you're actually trying to achieve. If I'm not the right person, I'll say so — I'd rather tell you in the first call than the third invoice.

- **A written scope** What gets built, what doesn't, what it costs, and when it lands. No code starts before we both agree on this document.

- **Build in visible increments** You get a working preview URL early and it updates continuously. No four-week silences ending in a surprise.

- **Launch with measurement wired in** Analytics, Search Console, and conversion tracking are part of the build, not a follow-up ticket. You can't iterate on what you aren't measuring.

- **Iterate over quarters** Organic growth is not a launch event. The sites I've grown got there through months of adding pages, fixing what underperformed, and doubling down on what ranked.

Questions

## Common questions

### Do you work with clients outside Israel?

Yes — most of my work is with US and European clients. I'm a native English speaker (American, University of Maryland), and Israel time zone overlaps a full working morning with Europe and the early afternoon with the US East Coast.

### How long until SEO work shows results?

Technical fixes can move rankings in days. Building genuine organic traffic on a new site takes quarters, not weeks — my own sites took months of consistent publishing before traffic became meaningful. Anyone promising you page one in 30 days is selling something else.

### Can you take over an existing codebase?

Regularly. A good portion of my professional work has been inheriting half-finished systems and getting them to production — legacy PHP, undocumented WordPress builds, and applications whose original developer is long gone.

### Are you available full time or freelance?

Both. I run my own SaaS products and take on select client work alongside them. If you're hiring for a founding or senior engineering role, that conversation is welcome too — my [resume is here](https://jacoborbach.com/Jacob_Orbach_CV.pdf).

### Who owns the code?

You do. Client work ships to your repository, your hosting, your accounts. No proprietary platform lock-in and no hostage situations if you later bring things in-house.

## Tell me what you're building

Send a couple of sentences about the project and what's currently in your way. I read every email and typically reply within 24 hours.

Page title: WordPress Maintenance & Care Plans – Updates, Backups, Fixes · Jacob Orbach

WordPress maintenance

# Your WordPress site, kept current and quietly working

A backup before every update. Tested on a staging copy when your host supports it. Someone who notices when it goes down.

I build WordPress for a living: plugins on WordPress.org, 30+ custom Gutenberg blocks, multilingual sites. So when an update breaks something, I fix the cause instead of rolling back and hoping. One monthly price, fix time included, no ticket queue.

Ask about your site

בעברית

$250

A month, up to 3 hours of fixes included

1 day

Response time, business days

100%

Of updates preceded by a backup

0

Lock-in: cancel with a month's notice

Every month

## What's included

### Updates, done safely

WordPress core, plugins and theme. Backed up first, tested on a staging copy when your host provides one, then applied to the live site and checked. Major versions (a big Elementor or WooCommerce jump) get extra care, and I tell you before I start.

### Backups you can restore

Regular automatic backups stored off your server, plus one before every change I make. A backup nobody has tested is a hope, so I check that they actually restore.

### Uptime & security

Monitoring that tells me when the site is down, SSL kept valid, security scanning, and removal of plugins and admin accounts that shouldn't be there anymore.

### Fix time

Up to 3 hours a month for the small things: a broken form, a layout glitch after an update, a slow page. Anything bigger is quoted first, and you decide.

### A short monthly report

What was updated, what I found, what I fixed, and anything you should know about. Plain English, one email.

### One person who knows your site

Not a rotating support desk. The same developer every month, who remembers why that plugin is there.

Why me

## A developer doing the upkeep

Most maintenance services are good at clicking "update" and bad at what happens when it breaks. I've been on the building side of WordPress for years:

- **Two plugins on WordPress.org,** one of them a WooCommerce payment gateway, so I know how plugins behave when WordPress or WooCommerce changes underneath them.

- **30+ custom Gutenberg blocks** for enterprise clients at a digital agency, plus Elementor sites and WPML multilingual builds with Hebrew RTL and English LTR.

- **Ongoing upkeep for a media organisation's three sites:** WordPress, Elementor and plugins kept current, DNS, SSL and caching across cPanel and Cloudflare, and the Search Console side. Including a site that was broken when I took it over.

- **A broken Elementor site rebuilt end to end** for a freelance client, with new pages designed on it.

**If an update breaks something, it's on me.** Because every change starts with a backup, the worst case is a quick restore, and fixing what the update broke comes out of my time, not your fix hours.

### Before we start

The monthly price is for a site in normal shape. If yours is badly out of date (years behind on WordPress or WooCommerce, or plugins that are no longer maintained), there's a one-time catch-up first, quoted after I look at it. That's where most of the risk sits, so I'd rather price it honestly than bury it in the monthly fee.

Questions

## Common questions

### What does it cost?

$250 a month, including up to 3 hours of fixes. In Israel, ₪500 a month plus VAT, including up to 2.5 hours. Extra work is quoted before I do it. A site that's badly out of date gets a one-time catch-up quote first.

### Do I have to move hosting?

No. I work with the hosting you already have. If it's causing problems (slow, unreliable, or overpriced), I'll tell you and suggest options, but moving is your call.

### What access do you need?

An administrator login for WordPress, your hosting panel, read access to your domain/DNS settings, and Cloudflare if you use it. You keep ownership of everything: your site, your hosting, your domain.

### How fast do you respond?

Within one business day. If the site is down, I look at it the same day during working hours.

### Can I cancel?

Anytime, with a month's notice. No contract term. If you leave, you get your latest backup and everything stays yours.

### Do you work with agencies?

Yes. If you build WordPress sites for clients and would rather not do the monthly upkeep, I can do it under your name, white label, with per-site pricing for agencies. Email me and we'll work out what fits.

### What counts as extra work?

New pages, new features, content and design changes, redesigns, and SEO projects. Those are quoted before I start. WooCommerce stores and multilingual sites are quoted separately, because there is more to keep working. Keeping what you have working and up to date is what the monthly fee covers.

בעברית

## תחזוקת אתר וורדפרס

**מענה תוך יום עסקים אחד.** **אם עדכון שובר משהו, משחזרים מגיבוי ומתקנים, בלי תוספת תשלום.**

אני מפתח וורדפרס: תוספים בספריית WordPress.org, מעל 30 בלוקים מותאמים לגוטנברג, אתרים רב-לשוניים עם RTL. כשעדכון שובר משהו, אני מתקן את הסיבה, לא רק מחזיר גרסה.

### מה כלול בכל חודש

- **עדכוני ליבה, תוספים וערכות נושא**, תמיד אחרי גיבוי. כשהאחסון מאפשר, בדיקה קודם על עותק של האתר (סביבת staging).

- **גיבוי לפני כל שינוי**, ובנוסף גיבוי אוטומטי קבוע מחוץ לשרת.

- **ניטור זמינות ומהירות**: התראה כשהאתר נופל, תעודת SSL תקינה.

- **סריקת אבטחה** והסרת תוספים ומשתמשים מיותרים.

- **תיקונים קטנים**: עד 2.5 שעות בחודש.

- **דוח חודשי קצר**: מה עודכן, מה נמצא ומה תוקן.

### מה לא כלול

שינויי תוכן ועיצוב, עמודים חדשים ואינטגרציות: 200 ₪ לשעה + מע״מ, בהצעת מחיר מראש. חנויות WooCommerce ואתרים רב-לשוניים מקבלים הצעת מחיר נפרדת.

**המחיר: 500 ₪ לחודש + מע״מ**, כולל עד 2.5 שעות תיקונים. חודשי, מראש, ביטול בהודעה של חודש. המחירים לא כוללים מע״מ. אתר שלא עודכן זמן רב מקבל קודם הצעת מחיר חד-פעמית להשלמת העדכונים.

### מה אני צריך מכם

משתמש מנהל בוורדפרס, גישה לפאנל האחסון, גישת צפייה להגדרות הדומיין (DNS), ו-Cloudflare אם יש. אין צורך להחליף אחסון: האתר, הדומיין והאחסון נשארים שלכם.

Page title: Payment Integration Developer – Stripe, Meshulam & Custom Gateways · Jacob Orbach

Payments

# Payment systems that reconcile at the end of the month

Taking money is easy. Taking it reliably, refunding it, invoicing it, and proving where it went is the actual work.

I've built payment infrastructure on three different kinds of rails — a card gateway processing over $1M a year (annualized), Stripe subscription billing for my own SaaS products, and an open-source cryptocurrency gateway for WooCommerce. Different rails, same hard parts: webhooks that arrive twice, states that get stuck, and edge cases that only show up with real money.

Discuss a payments project

See the systems

$1M+

A year in payments, annualized

3

Payment rails: cards, subscriptions, crypto

2

Open-source payment packages published

90%

Faster contract turnaround via e-signatures

Scope

## What I integrate

### Stripe billing & subscriptions

Checkout, subscriptions, plan changes, proration, failed-payment recovery, and the webhook handling that keeps your database agreeing with Stripe's.

### Meshulam & Israeli gateways

Full Meshulam SDK integration including tokenization, recurring charges, and invoice generation — built into a Strapi backend and running in production.

### Custom WooCommerce gateways

When your processor has no plugin, or the one that exists is abandoned. Written to the WooCommerce gateway API properly, so refunds and order states behave.

### Cryptocurrency payments

Non-custodial crypto acceptance where funds go straight to the merchant's own wallet. Address derivation, confirmation monitoring, and order reconciliation.

### Invoicing & documents

Automated PDF invoice generation, e-signature flows, and the document trail your finance team and auditors will ask for.

### Rescue & reconciliation

Payments landing but orders not updating. Duplicate charges. Webhooks silently failing for three weeks. I find it and fix it.

Proof

## Systems handling real money

### Meshulam + Strapi — $1M+ per year, annualized

At One Digital I built an end-to-end payment system on the Meshulam SDK inside a Strapi backend, processing **over $1,000,000 a year in transaction volume**. The interesting half was never the charge call. It was everything that has to stay true afterwards:

- **Webhook reconciliation.** Gateways retry. They deliver out of order, they deliver twice, and occasionally they deliver three weeks late. Getting a replayed webhook to update the order it already created, instead of creating a second one, is most of the work in any payment integration.

- **Lifecycle hooks as the single source of truth.** Order state transitions live in Strapi lifecycle hooks rather than scattered through controllers, so a payment can't be marked paid down one code path and left pending down another.

- **Invoices generated automatically.** Dockerized Puppeteer on Azure Functions renders the PDF invoice as part of the payment flow, not as a monthly chore, which is the difference between finance trusting the system and finance keeping a parallel spreadsheet.

### Stripe — billing my own SaaS, in production

[GhostChat](https://ghostchat.dev/) and [Gmailytics](https://gmailytics.com/) run on Stripe subscription billing I built and still operate. Two decisions there are worth stealing for any subscription product:

- **Entitlements resolve from the subscription itself.** What a customer can do is derived from the Stripe price they're actually on, not from a plan name copied into your own database at signup. Those two drift apart the first time someone upgrades mid-cycle, and once they drift you are reconciling access by hand.

- **Repricing is a new Price, not a migration.** Because entitlement is read from the subscription itself, changing what you charge means publishing a new Price object rather than running a script against live customers at 2am — and you decide deliberately, per entitlement, which existing subscribers move.

There is a particular kind of care you develop when the failed-payment webhook is your own revenue, and that's the standard I bring to client billing systems.

### KaspaWoo — open-source crypto gateway

A production Kaspa payment gateway for WooCommerce, open-sourced on [GitHub](https://github.com/jacoborbach/kaspa-payments-gateway-woocommerce). It's non-custodial: payments derive to the merchant's own wallet, never mine. The address derivation had to be its own package because no lightweight JavaScript option existed — the official tooling is a WASM build far too heavy to sit inside a WordPress plugin — so I wrote [kaspa-simple-wallet](https://www.npmjs.com/package/kaspa-simple-wallet) in pure JS and published it MIT: watch-only derivation from a KPUB/XPUB, Kaspium-compatible, so the store never holds a private key. It is written to the WooCommerce gateway API properly, which means refunds and order states behave the way the rest of the admin expects them to.

**Why the non-custodial detail matters:** a store that never holds keys can't lose them. Most payment bugs are really state bugs — and the best fix is usually an architecture where the dangerous state doesn't exist in your system at all.

### E-signatures and contract flow

At Hertz Furniture I integrated SignNow for e-signatures on PDF quotes, cutting contract turnaround time by 90%. Payments rarely live alone — they sit next to quotes, contracts, invoices, and a CRM that all need to agree with each other.

## Got a payments problem?

New integration, custom gateway, or something that's quietly broken and costing you orders — describe it and I'll tell you what it'll take.

Page title: Custom AI Integration – LLM Features, Agents & Chatbots · Jacob Orbach

Custom AI Integration

# AI features that survive contact with real users

The demo is the easy part. Making it cheap, safe, and accurate on live traffic is the job.

I build LLM features into real products — support agents that actually answer, retrieval grounded in your own content, and model routing that keeps the bill from tripling when you grow. I run this in production on my own SaaS, on paying customers' traffic, which is why I know where it breaks.

Discuss an AI build

See what I've shipped

Live

Claude responder in production

MIT

Open-source agent runner on npm

3

LLM providers supported

~15KB

SDK it ships inside

Scope

## What I build

### AI support & sales agents

Chat agents that answer from your knowledge base, your product pages, and your docs — and hand off to a human on the questions where a wrong answer would cost you a customer.

### Grounded answers over your content

Retrieval pipelines so the model answers from your actual content instead of inventing plausible fiction. Includes the unglamorous part: chunking, freshness, and citation.

### AI inside an existing product

Summarization, classification, extraction, drafting, semantic search. Bolted onto the app you already have, without a rewrite and without a new vendor platform.

### Internal tooling & automation

The workflows eating your team's week — triaging tickets, parsing documents, enriching records, generating first drafts of things a human then approves.

Proof

## Running in production, not in a notebook

### GhostChat AI — live on customer traffic

[GhostChat](https://ghostchat.dev/) is my privacy-first chat SaaS. Its AI responder runs on Claude via the Anthropic API, answering real visitor messages on paying customers' websites — grounded in each site's own knowledge base and behaviour prompt, on Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects for per-conversation state. The widget on this page is that product.

The parts that took the longest are the ones demos skip:

- **Grounding that refuses to guess.** The model answers from the site's own FAQ knowledge base and stays inside it. Getting a confident model to say "I'll get someone to answer that" instead of inventing a plausible policy is a prompt-and-retrieval problem, and it is most of the work.

- **Handoff that doesn't strand anyone.** When the agent hits a question it shouldn't answer, it hands off to a human — and if nobody is online, it says when the team is actually back, in the owner's own wording and the owner's own timezone. Every unattended handoff is a lead you already paid for.

- **A unit cost you can defend.** Replies land around a third of a cent each. Knowing that number is what lets you offer AI on every plan instead of hiding it behind an enterprise tier, and it comes from model choice and prompt size, not from wishful pricing.

- **Per-site isolation.** Each site gets its own knowledge base, its own behaviour prompt, and its own limits, because one customer's tone and another's compliance rules are not the same product.

### ghostchat-agent — open-source, bring your own model

I publish [ghostchat-agent](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ghostchat-agent) on npm (MIT licensed) so teams can run their own AI on their own infrastructure: their model, their server, their data. It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, and local Ollama models behind one webhook interface, with a setup wizard that provisions the whole thing in a couple of minutes.

**The part I'd point a client to first:** that package's README opens with a security warning, not a feature list. It tells you to run the agent in an isolated folder with no access to your codebase or databases, and explains why — visitor messages are untrusted input from the public internet, and an agent with filesystem access is a prompt-injection target.

Most AI integrations ship without anyone having thought about that. It's the first thing I design for.

### Cost-controlled model routing

The failure mode nobody warns you about is the invoice. Sending every message to a frontier model is how a working prototype becomes an unaffordable product at scale.

I architect these systems to classify each request and route it to the cheapest model that can actually handle it. Simple turns — greetings, FAQ-answerable questions, follow-ups already covered by context in the conversation — go to a small fast model. Only the turns that genuinely need retrieval or hard synthesis escalate to a larger one, and once the retrieved context is in the conversation history, follow-ups drop back down. That routing decision is per-message, not per-conversation, and it is usually the difference between an AI feature that pays for itself and one that gets switched off after the first big bill.

Hard-Won

## Four things that sink AI features

These are the issues that show up in month two, after the demo has already been approved.

- **Unbounded cost** No routing, no caching, no token ceilings. Works fine at 100 messages a day and becomes indefensible at 10,000. Fixed by routing and hard limits designed in from the start.

- **Confident wrong answers** A model with no grounding will invent a refund policy you don't have. Fixed by retrieval over your real content plus explicit handoff rules for questions where being wrong is expensive.

- **Prompt injection** Anything a visitor types is hostile input. An agent wired to your tools, files, or database without sandboxing is a live vulnerability, not a feature.

- **No way to tell if it's working** Without logging, evaluation cases, and a review loop, "is the AI any good?" becomes a matter of opinion. I wire measurement in before launch so the answer stays factual.

Stack

## What I work with

### Models & providers

Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, and self-hosted Ollama models. Provider-agnostic by default so you aren't locked to one vendor's pricing.

### Application layer

Node.js, TypeScript, React, Next.js, Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, Supabase, PostgreSQL with vector search.

### Around the model

Retrieval and chunking, streaming responses, webhook architectures, evaluation harnesses, cost and latency instrumentation.
